The judgment referred to above inter alia holds that for attracting the penal provisions of Section
30(a), 30(g) of the Bihar Prohibition and Excise Act, 2016, the substance must be an intoxicant or a
liquor which could be served as an alcohol or as a substitute of alcohol which is capable of being
used or consumed for getting intoxicated.
The petitioner/company contends that the lab report of the Excise Chemist which is the very basis
for Patna High Court CR. WJC No.366 of 2021 dt.09-02-2022 initiating this prosecution is incorrect
and such report ought not to have been taken as sacrosanct.
For testing the ethyl alcohol content in a beverage FSSAI has prescribed a standard set of guidelines
for detecting the ethyl alcohol content. Those guidelines have been completely ignored while testing
the sample and therefore the report by him is only a hasty conclusion.

petitioner/company was tested for ethyl alcohol at Mysore which certified that it had zero percent

Private Limited and Vimta which also reported zero percent alcohol in such sample. Patna High

guidelines provided by the FSSAI but no heed was paid to such request.
The Bureau of Indian Standards has come out with a second revision of the methods of test for
alcoholic drinks.
There are three methods of testing for the purposes of determination of ethyl alcohol content has
been provided in such standard.
Patna High Court CR. WJC No.366 of 2021 dt.09-02-2022 The first method is a routine method for
testing the apparent strength. The second method is known as referee method which tests the real
strength and the third method is used only in cases of those alcoholic drinks which yield volatile oil
on distillation.
The methods prescribed by the BIS specifies the apparatus which is to be used and the procedure for
testing and also for calculation of the content.
There is nothing on record to indicate that such process was followed by the Chemical Examiner of
the Excise Department of Government of Bihar at Patna and therefore such report ought not to be
treated as a final report for launching prosecution against anyone.
In State of Haryana & Others Vs. Bhajan Lal and Others reported in Supp(1) SCC 335, a two Judges
Bench of the Supreme Court provided an illustrative set of situations, where the High Court could
exercise its jurisdiction under Article 226 of the Constitution of India Patna High Court CR. WJC
No.366 of 2021 dt.09-02-2022 or Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure for quashing the
FIR.
One of the conditions provided is that if the allegations made in the FIR, if taken on its face value
and accepted in its entirety does not prima facie constitute any offence or make out any case against
the accused, such subject FIR can be quashed.
In a more recent decision of the Supreme Court in Neeharika Infrastructure Pvt. Ltd. v. State of
Maharashtra and Others (2021) SCC OnLine SC 315 , the Supreme Court has reiterated those
principles but has cautioned that the investigation ought not to be thwarted and the power of
quashing the FIR should be exercised sparingly with circumspection.
The prosecution of the petitioner in the instant case is on a finding that some of the samples which
were seized contained more ethyl alcohol than the tolerance limit. If the articles, so seized, were not
sold as intoxicants or could be consumed as intoxicants, it would not fall Patna High Court CR. WJC

texts.facts_text:
This writ petition has been filed for quashing the entire prosecution emanating out of Pandaul P.S. Case No. 270 of 2020 instituted for the offences under Sections 30(a) and 35(e) of the Bihar Prohibition and Excise Act, 2016 and under Sections 272, 273, 465 and 420 of the Indian Penal Code. The petitioner is a Company incorporated under the provisions of the Companies Act which is engaged in the manufacture of non-alcoholic beers/drinks at Naubatpur in the district of Patna. The prosecution against the petitioner/company has been challenged on the ground that none of the offences under the Indian Penal Code or under the Bihar Prohibition and Excise Act, 2016 was made out and that the petitioner/company has never manufactured or sold any intoxicant or liquor as defined under the Excise Act.

The petitioner, United Breweries Limited, sells non-alcoholic beverages named Kingfisher Radler and Kingfisher Ultra. These drinks are certified as non-alcoholic by the Bureau of Indian Standards, which mandates less than 0.5% ethyl alcohol by volume. The product was tested at the CSIR-Central Food Technological Research Institute, Mysore, and reported as zero percent alcohol. However, the Chemical Examiner of the Excise Department at Patna reported the sample as having 0.8% v/v alcohol, leading to a prosecution.

The subject FIR was initiated based on a lab report by the Excise Chemist indicating that some of the samples seized contained more ethyl alcohol than the tolerance limit. The products were tested for ethyl alcohol content at Mysore, which certified zero percent alcohol. Further tests by NABL accredited laboratories also reported zero percent alcohol. The Bureau of Indian Standards has specified three methods for testing ethyl alcohol content, none of which were followed by the Chemical Examiner of the Excise Department.
texts.arguments_petitioner:
The petitioner/company has been brewing malt-based non-alcoholic drinks strictly in accordance with Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS) and only after grant of a license issued by Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) for manufacture and sale of such non-alcoholic beverage. After the imposition of prohibition in the State of Bihar on sale and consumption of foreign liquor and beer from 5th of April, 2016, the petitioner/company was required to seek permission from the Excise and Prohibition Department, Government of Bihar for manufacturing malt-based non-alcoholic drinks and on such request to the Excise Department, the license was given on 13.12.2016 by the Excise Commissioner, Bihar. Again by notification dated 24.01.2017, the petitioner/company was permitted to engage in the manufacture of non-alcoholic beverages.

The Excise Act defines intoxicant and liquor under Sections 2(40) and 2(44). An intoxicant is a liquor served as alcohol or its substitute and consumed for intoxication. A non-alcoholic drink should contain less than 0.5% v/v alcohol. The prosecution was launched based on a single report, ignoring potential reasons for higher alcohol content, such as further fermentation.

The petitioner argues that the lab report by the Excise Chemist is incorrect and should not be considered sacrosanct. The FSSAI guidelines for testing ethyl alcohol content were ignored, making the report a hasty conclusion. The petitioner's products were tested by multiple NABL accredited laboratories, all reporting zero percent alcohol. The prosecution is based on a finding that some samples contained more ethyl alcohol than the tolerance limit, but if the articles were not sold as intoxicants, they do not fall under the prohibited category.
texts.reasoning_text:
The petitioner argues that the prosecution was inappropriate based solely on the report of the Chemical Examiner, without considering other factors that could have led to the higher alcohol content. They claim that even if the sample had more than 0.5% v/v alcohol, it was not consumed for intoxication, which is a necessary condition for the beverage to fall under the prohibition.

The court notes that the Prohibition Act does not prohibit the sale of non-alcoholic substances that conform to BIS standards. The penal provisions of the Bihar Prohibition and Excise Act, 2016 apply only to substances that are intoxicants or substitutes of alcohol. The prosecution is based on a finding that some samples contained more ethyl alcohol than the tolerance limit, but if the articles were not sold as intoxicants, they do not fall under the prohibited category.
texts.decision_text: For the reasons stated, the subject FIR viz. Pandaul P.S. Case No. 270 of 2020 is quashed. All other prosecutions emanating from the FIR are also quashed. The application stands allowed.

key_facts_bullets: Petitioner is a company engaged in the manufacture of non-alcoholic beers/drinks at Naubatpur in Patna.
Prosecution is for offences under Sections 30(a) and 35(e) of the Bihar Prohibition and Excise Act, 2016 and Sections 272, 273, 465,
Petitioner sells non-alcoholic beverages named Kingfisher Radler and Kingfisher Ultra.
Bureau of Indian Standards mandates less than 0.5% ethyl alcohol by volume for non-alcoholic drinks.
CSIR-Central Food Technological Research Institute reported the drink as zero percent alcohol.
Excise Department reported the sample as having 0.8% v/v alcohol, leading to prosecution.
Subject FIR was based on a lab report indicating higher ethyl alcohol content than the tolerance limit.
Products tested by multiple labs reported zero percent alcohol.
Bureau of Indian Standards has specified three methods for testing ethyl alcohol content.
issues_bullets: Whether the prosecution against the petitioner for offences under Sections 30(a) and 35(e) of the Bihar Prohibition and Excise Act, 2016 and Sections 272, 273, 465, and 420 of the Indian Penal Code is justified.
Whether the petitioner has manufactured or sold any intoxicant or liquor as defined under the Excise Act.
Definition of intoxicant and liquor under the Excise Act.
Validity of prosecution based on a single report.
Consideration of potential reasons for higher alcohol content.
Validity of the lab report by the Excise Chemist.
Compliance with FSSAI guidelines for testing ethyl alcohol content.
Whether the products fall under the prohibited category of liquor.
holdings_bullets: The prosecution against the petitioner for the mentioned offences is not justified as the petitioner has not manufactured or sold any intoxicant or liquor as defined under the Excise Act.
The Prohibition Act does not prohibit the sale of non-alcoholic substances that conform to BIS standards.
Penal provisions apply only to substances that are intoxicants or substitutes of alcohol.
Prosecution is not warranted if the articles were not sold as intoxicants.
